Unbiased estimates of the reliability of the four bipolar scales must await a cross-validation.

The use of photographic simulations rather than actual environments, while convenient and controlled, may not fully capture responses to real environments.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper describes the development and validation of scales to assess the affective quality attributed to physical environments. It proposes a two-dimensional bipolar space (pleasant-unpleasant and arousing-sleepy) with a circular ordering of eight affective terms. The study developed and refined eight unipolar and four 10-item bipolar scales (arousing-sleepy, exciting-gloomy, pleasant-unpleasant, distressing-relaxing). Empirical results demonstrated that these scales are reliable (Cronbach's alpha ranging from .72 to .94), and principal components analysis confirmed a two-dimensional structure accounting for over 82% of the total variance. Intercorrelations among the scales largely conformed to the hypothesized circular ordering, and the pleasant-unpleasant and arousing-sleepy scales effectively predicted the other two bipolar scales (R=.84 and .87). High interrater reliability (r=.97) was also found for the pleasant-unpleasant and arousing-sleepy scales when applied to environmental photographs. Limitations include the geographical restriction of the sample to Vancouver and the need for further cross-validation of the bipolar scales.
